stem: After a workstation compromise, an attacker moved freely to servers across the same flat internal network. Which architectural change BEST limits this lateral movement in the future?
options: Deploying a stronger firewall at the Internet edge
Enforcing longer passwords on all workstations
Segmenting the network and restricting traffic between zones
Increasing logging on the core switches
explanations: The perimeter firewall never sees east-west traffic between internal hosts, which is where the attacker moved.
Password strength does not change which systems a compromised workstation can reach over the network.
Zoning the network and filtering inter-zone traffic confines a compromise to its segment, directly limiting lateral movement.
More logging improves detection after the fact but places no barrier in the attacker's path.

stem: In a three-tier web application exposed to the Internet, where should the database server be positioned?
options: In an internal zone reachable only from the application tier
In the DMZ alongside the public web servers
On the public subnet behind a host firewall
On the same VLAN as user workstations
explanations: The database belongs in the most protected zone, accepting connections solely from the application tier that legitimately needs it.
The DMZ is semi-trusted and Internet-adjacent; a web-server compromise there would sit directly beside the data.
Public placement exposes the database to the Internet with only a single local layer of defense.
User VLANs are a common phishing entry point; any compromised workstation would have direct network reach to the database.

stem: Users on an office VLAN intermittently receive network settings from an unauthorized device, which routes their traffic through an attacker-controlled gateway. Which switch feature MOST directly prevents this?
options: Port security limiting MAC addresses per port
DHCP snooping with trusted ports
Spanning Tree Protocol root guard
802.1X port-based network access control
explanations: Port security caps how many MAC addresses a port may learn; the rogue device answers DHCP queries from its single, legitimate-looking address.
DHCP snooping classifies ports as trusted or untrusted and drops server-style DHCP offers arriving on untrusted ports — precisely the rogue-server case.
Root guard protects the spanning-tree topology from rogue root bridges; it does not inspect DHCP traffic.
802.1X keeps unauthenticated devices off the network, but an authenticated yet compromised host can still hand out rogue leases; snooping blocks the offers themselves.

stem: Two branch offices must protect all traffic exchanged between their networks across the Internet, including concealing the original internal IP headers. Which configuration meets this requirement?
options: IPsec ESP in transport mode between the gateways
IPsec AH in tunnel mode between the sites
TLS on each application crossing the link
IPsec ESP in tunnel mode between the site gateways
explanations: Transport mode protects only the payload and leaves the original IP header exposed; between gateways it also cannot carry other hosts' traffic.
AH authenticates but does not encrypt, so the traffic and internal headers remain readable in transit.
Per-application TLS covers only the applications configured for it and does nothing to conceal internal addressing.
Tunnel-mode ESP encrypts the entire original packet — payload and internal headers — inside a new outer packet between the gateways.

stem: Remote employees reach corporate systems through a VPN, while their other web traffic bypasses the tunnel and goes straight to the Internet. What is the PRIMARY security concern with this split-tunnel arrangement?
options: Encryption strength drops when the tunnel is split
Split tunnels consume extra VPN bandwidth
The device can bridge Internet threats into the corporate network
Users lose access to internal resources
explanations: The tunnel's cryptography is unchanged; splitting affects routing, not cipher strength.
Split tunneling reduces VPN bandwidth use, since general browsing bypasses the concentrator.
Traffic to the open Internet bypasses corporate inspection, so a device compromised on that path becomes a bridge into the private network over its tunnel.
Internal resources remain reachable through the tunnel; carrying them is exactly what the tunnel does.

stem: A utility connects its plant control network to the corporate IT network for production reporting, but engineering workstations must never be directly reachable from the business side. Which design BEST enforces this?
options: A brokered intermediary zone that terminates all cross-boundary flows
Separate VLANs for IT and OT on the shared core switches
Host-based firewalls on each engineering workstation
Encryption of all traffic passing between IT and OT
explanations: An industrial DMZ terminates every cross-boundary connection at brokered services, so business systems reach the broker — never the engineering workstations themselves.
VLANs on shared fabric are logical separation only; a misconfiguration or VLAN-hopping technique reopens the path to the control network.
Endpoint firewalls depend on every workstation staying correctly configured; a single lapse re-exposes it, so they cannot serve as the enforced boundary.
Encrypting the traffic protects its confidentiality but does not restrict which systems can reach the workstations at all.

stem: A security analyst discovers that an attacker on a user-facing access port sent traffic into a restricted VLAN by crafting frames with two 802.1Q tags. Which switch configuration change BEST prevents this double-tagging attack?
options: Enable dynamic trunking negotiation on all access ports so the switch controls trunk formation
Assign the native VLAN on trunk links to an unused VLAN ID and hard-code user ports as access ports
Configure DHCP snooping so untrusted ports cannot deliver tagged frames into the network
Apply port mirroring to copy access-port traffic to a monitoring VLAN for inspection
explanations: This inverts the control: Dynamic Trunking Protocol is what lets an attacker negotiate a trunk from a user port, so it should be disabled on access ports, not enabled.
Double tagging only works when the attacker's access VLAN matches the trunk's native VLAN; moving the native VLAN to an unused ID and statically configuring access ports removes both preconditions.
DHCP snooping validates DHCP messages to stop rogue address servers; it does not examine or block 802.1Q tag manipulation in ordinary data frames.
Port mirroring (SPAN) is a detective monitoring feature that copies traffic for analysis; it does nothing to stop the tagged frames from reaching the restricted VLAN.

stem: A hospital wants to ensure that only managed, corporate-owned devices can connect to wired network ports in public waiting areas, where visitors can physically reach the jacks. Which control BEST meets this requirement?
options: MAC address filtering maintained on each access switch
Placing all waiting-area ports in a guest VLAN with Internet-only access
802.1X port-based authentication using certificates issued to corporate devices
Physically locking network jacks and disabling all unused wall ports
explanations: MAC filtering is easily defeated because an attacker can observe a legitimate device's address and spoof it; a MAC address authenticates nothing.
A guest VLAN isolates whatever plugs in but still grants network access; the requirement is to admit only managed devices, which demands authentication rather than mere containment.
Port-based network access control with certificate-based EAP (such as EAP-TLS) cryptographically proves the connecting device holds a corporate-issued credential before the port passes any traffic.
Physical locks reduce casual tampering but cannot stop someone who reaches an active jack, and ports needed by staff must remain enabled; nothing verifies what actually connects.

stem: A small office currently uses WPA2-Personal with a shared passphrase on its wireless network. The owner asks what security benefit an upgrade to WPA3-Personal would provide. Which improvement is MOST significant?
options: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals resists offline dictionary attacks against captured handshakes
It replaces the shared passphrase with per-user credentials tied to a RADIUS server
It introduces AES encryption, which WPA2 did not support
It hides the SSID so attackers can no longer discover the network name
explanations: WPA3-Personal replaces the WPA2 four-way handshake, whose captures can be brute-forced offline, with SAE, a password-authenticated key exchange that forces active per-guess interaction and adds forward secrecy.
Per-user credentials with a RADIUS back end describe WPA3-Enterprise built on 802.1X; WPA3-Personal still uses a shared passphrase.
WPA2 already mandated AES-CCMP; it was WPA and WEP that relied on RC4-based protection, so AES is not new in WPA3.
SSID cloaking is an unrelated and largely cosmetic setting; the network name is still exposed in probe and association traffic regardless of WPA version.

stem: An external scan shows a customer-facing payment portal still accepts TLS 1.0 connections for legacy browser compatibility, though analytics show fewer than 0.1 percent of clients use it. As security manager, what should you recommend FIRST?
options: Deploy a web application firewall rule to inspect TLS 1.0 sessions for attack signatures
Disable TLS 1.0 and 1.1 on the portal after a short notice period to the residual client base
Direct the application team to migrate every internal service to TLS 1.3 simultaneously
Accept the risk formally, since fewer than 0.1 percent of connections are affected
explanations: A web application firewall cannot fix a protocol-level weakness; downgrade and cryptographic attacks against TLS 1.0 occur below the layer where WAF signatures operate.

The business impact is negligible while the exposure and compliance impact (PCI DSS prohibits early TLS for cardholder data) are significant, so retiring the deprecated versions with brief customer notice is the risk-based choice.
Forcing a simultaneous TLS 1.3 migration everywhere conflates the urgent external exposure with a much larger internal modernization effort and would delay the actual fix.
Risk acceptance is inappropriate when a low-cost remediation exists and the deprecated protocol violates industry mandates for payment environments.

stem: A SaaS provider's traffic was briefly routed through an unrelated foreign network after another autonomous system announced a more specific BGP prefix covering the provider's address space. Which measure BEST reduces the chance of a recurrence?
options: Enable MD5 authentication on all BGP peering sessions with adjacent providers
Require TLS for all customer connections so intercepted traffic remains unreadable
Publish route origin authorizations for its prefixes and use transit providers that drop RPKI-invalid announcements
Advertise more specific prefixes continuously so competing announcements never win best-path selection
explanations: Session authentication (MD5 or TCP-AO) protects an individual BGP session against spoofed segments between two peers; it cannot stop a distant autonomous system from originating a false route.
TLS limits what a hijacker can read but does nothing to prevent the outage and traffic-diversion risk of the routes themselves being drawn to the wrong network.
ROAs let networks performing RPKI route origin validation recognize that the more specific announcement came from an unauthorized origin AS and discard it, addressing the actual hijack mechanism.
Permanent maximal deaggregation bloats global routing tables and still ties with an equally specific hijack; it treats a symptom instead of enabling origin validation.

stem: After a DNS cache-poisoning incident redirected employees to a counterfeit payroll portal, an architect proposes deploying DNSSEC validation on the enterprise resolvers. Which outcome should management expect this control to deliver?
options: Queries and responses will be encrypted, hiding employees' lookups from eavesdroppers
Known-malicious domains will be blocked through signed reputation feeds
Zone transfers will require mutually authenticated TLS sessions between servers
Resolvers will be able to verify that answers are authentic and unmodified via digital signatures
explanations: Encrypted transport is what DNS over TLS or DNS over HTTPS provides; DNSSEC leaves queries and answers fully readable on the wire.
Blocking bad domains is a DNS filtering or response policy zone capability; DNSSEC validates legitimate data rather than judging domain reputation.
Zone transfer protection is normally achieved with TSIG keys or access restrictions; DNSSEC imposes no TLS requirement between authoritative servers.
DNSSEC signs resource records so a validating resolver detects forged or tampered answers such as poisoned cache entries, directly countering the incident's attack vector.

stem: A company adopting zero trust currently grants full intranet access to any device that connects through the campus LAN or the VPN. Which core principle should the new architecture apply in place of this assumption?
options: Access decisions must be made per session based on identity, device posture, and context rather than network location
All internal traffic must be blocked until the perimeter firewall is replaced with a next-generation model
Users on the corporate LAN may retain implicit trust while only VPN users are continuously re-authenticated
Encrypting all internal traffic between endpoints is sufficient to establish trust
explanations: Zero trust removes implicit trust derived from network placement; every access request is evaluated against verified identity, device health, and context, and is re-evaluated continuously.
Zero trust is an architectural principle, not a firewall product upgrade; replacing the perimeter appliance still leaves location-based trust intact behind it.
Exempting LAN users preserves exactly the implicit location-based trust that zero trust is designed to eliminate; inside and outside are treated alike.
An encrypted channel protects data in transit but says nothing about whether the requesting subject should be authorized; trust requires verified identity and posture, not just cryptography.

stem: A team configured an IPsec VPN to a partner using Authentication Header, but the tunnel fails whenever traffic passes through the branch office's NAT gateway. The partner also requires confidentiality for the data. What should the team do?
options: Replace the NAT gateway with static one-to-one address mappings so AH integrity checks remain valid
Switch AH from tunnel mode to transport mode so the outer header is no longer protected
Use ESP with NAT traversal, which provides integrity and confidentiality and tolerates address translation
Encapsulate the AH tunnel inside GRE so the translated header is hidden from the integrity check
explanations: Even a static mapping still rewrites the IP addresses that AH includes in its integrity calculation, so the hash verification still fails on arrival.

Mode choice does not fix this: AH authenticates immutable IP header fields in both transport and tunnel modes, so translation still invalidates the check, and AH provides no encryption in either mode.
ESP does not authenticate the outer IP header and supports NAT traversal via UDP encapsulation, so it survives address translation while also supplying the encryption AH inherently lacks.
GRE is plain encapsulation with no cryptographic protection of its own, and layering AH across a translated path recreates the same header-modification failure.

stem: A retailer is replacing its MPLS circuits with SD-WAN that sends branch traffic over local broadband Internet links, including direct breakout to cloud applications. Which consideration is MOST important for the security architecture?
options: Preserving MPLS-equivalent quality of service so voice and video traffic does not degrade
Ensuring branch routers have capacity to carry full Internet BGP routing tables
Consolidating branch firewalls into the SD-WAN controller, which now centrally enforces all policy
Protecting traffic that now rides the public Internet with authenticated encrypted tunnels and inspection at cloud breakout points
explanations: Quality of service is a legitimate performance concern, but it addresses availability of media quality, not the confidentiality and integrity exposure created by leaving the private carrier network.
SD-WAN overlays use tunnels to defined endpoints and default routes; branches do not ingest full BGP feeds, so this is a capacity myth rather than the design issue.
The controller orchestrates policy but does not itself inspect branch traffic; direct Internet breakout increases, not decreases, the need for local or cloud-delivered security enforcement.

MPLS gave traffic separation on a private backbone; once branches use broadband and reach the cloud directly, IPsec-based overlay encryption and security inspection at breakout points must supply the protection the carrier implicitly provided.

stem: Finance staff keep receiving convincing invoice emails that spoof the company's own domain in the visible From header. SPF is already published. Which addition BEST enables receiving servers to reject these forged messages?
options: Publish a DMARC reject policy with DKIM signing so receivers verify alignment with the visible From domain
Tighten the SPF record to a hard-fail qualifier so unauthorized sending hosts are refused
Deploy S/MIME certificates to all finance employees so their outbound mail is digitally signed
Enable opportunistic TLS between mail gateways to stop interception of messages in transit
explanations: DMARC ties SPF and DKIM results to the From domain the user actually sees and publishes the owner's instruction to reject failures, which is precisely what defeats display-From spoofing at scale.
SPF, even with a hard fail, evaluates the envelope sender (MAIL FROM), which attackers can set to a domain they control while still forging the visible From header the user reads.
S/MIME authenticates individual senders to recipients who validate signatures, but receiving servers will not reject the forged mail, and external counterparties rarely check such signatures.
TLS between gateways protects messages from eavesdropping in transit; it makes no assertion about who the sender is and cannot cause forged mail to be rejected.

stem: A company deploying VoIP wants to keep the audio content of calls confidential as it crosses the office network. Which protocol is specifically designed to provide this protection?
options: SIP over TLS
RTP
SRTP
explanations: TLS-protected SIP secures call setup signaling, such as session negotiation and dialed identities, but does not encrypt the voice media stream itself.
RTP is the transport that carries the audio, but it carries the media in cleartext; it is the protocol being protected, not the protection.
H.323 is an alternative signaling and control suite for multimedia sessions; like SIP it manages calls rather than encrypting their audio content.
Secure Real-time Transport Protocol encrypts and integrity-protects the media stream, keeping the spoken content of calls confidential on the network.

stem: An HVAC vendor needs recurring remote access to maintenance servers on the facilities network. Today a technician connects through a shared desktop-sharing tool installed on an engineer's workstation. Which redesign BEST manages this third-party connectivity?
options: Issue the vendor a standard employee VPN profile so sessions traverse the corporate remote access concentrator
Route vendor sessions through a dedicated jump host with MFA, individual accounts, session recording, and access scoped to the maintenance servers
Keep the desktop-sharing tool but restrict its use to business hours through firewall schedules
Require the vendor to sign a connection agreement documenting their security obligations and liability
explanations: A general-purpose employee VPN grants a third party broad network reachability and mixes their traffic with staff access, violating least privilege for third-party connectivity.

A brokered jump host with individually authenticated accounts, MFA, recording, and tightly scoped destinations enforces least privilege and accountability, the core requirements for vendor remote access.
Scheduling narrows the window of exposure but leaves an unmanaged, shared-credential access path in place; the fundamental weaknesses of accountability and scope remain.
Agreements set expectations and transfer liability but are purely administrative; they do not technically constrain or monitor what the vendor can actually reach.

stem: An online brokerage's 10 Gbps Internet links were saturated for hours by a 300 Gbps reflection flood; on-premises appliances never saw manageable load. Management asks how to withstand a repeat event. Which approach is MOST effective?
options: Upgrade the perimeter firewalls to higher-throughput models with SYN flood protection features
Implement rate limiting and geographic blocking ACLs on the enterprise border routers
Increase Internet capacity to 40 Gbps spread across redundant carriers and diverse paths
Engage an upstream cloud scrubbing or CDN-based mitigation service that filters attack traffic before it reaches the enterprise links
explanations: Firewall capacity is irrelevant once the access circuits are saturated upstream of the appliance; the flood must be dropped before it ever reaches the enterprise edge.
Border-router controls act only after the flood has already consumed the inbound circuits, and reflection sources are globally distributed, making geographic blocks largely ineffective.
Adding bandwidth is an arms race the defender loses; 40 Gbps still fails against a 300 Gbps flood while multiplying recurring circuit costs.
Only a mitigation provider with aggregate capacity exceeding the attack, diverting traffic via BGP or DNS into scrubbing centers, can absorb volumetric floods and forward clean traffic downstream.

stem: During an incident investigation, analysts find timestamps across firewalls, servers, and domain controllers differ by minutes, and one syslog source is hours off, making event correlation unreliable. Which design change BEST prevents this problem?
options: Configure each device to poll any public NTP pool server of its administrator's choosing
Synchronize device clocks manually during quarterly maintenance windows
Deploy a redundant internal time hierarchy traceable to trusted references, with authenticated NTP required for all logging devices
Compensate in the SIEM by applying a per-source clock offset to timestamps as events are ingested
explanations: Independent polling of arbitrary public servers yields inconsistent references, no authentication, and exposure to spoofed time; a coherent managed hierarchy is what creates consistency.
Manually set clocks are guaranteed to drift between visits, and minutes of skew is exactly what breaks log correlation and Kerberos time tolerances.
A managed internal stratum design synchronized to reliable sources, with authentication so devices reject forged time updates, keeps every log source on a single trustworthy timeline.
Offsets applied at ingestion mask the symptom: they go stale as clocks continue drifting, and Kerberos, certificate validation, and unlogged systems still suffer from bad local time.

stem: A firewall protecting a cardholder-data enclave suffers a software crash. By design, no traffic may pass while the device is down, even though this interrupts business transactions until service is restored. Which principle does this design illustrate?
options: Fail secure (fail closed)
Fail open
Graceful degradation
High availability
explanations: Blocking all traffic during a failure preserves confidentiality and integrity at the cost of availability, which is the definition of failing secure for a control guarding sensitive data.
Fail open would pass traffic uninspected during the outage, prioritizing availability over protection, which is the opposite of this design decision.
Graceful degradation keeps reduced functionality running through a fault; here service is deliberately halted entirely rather than partially maintained.
High availability uses redundancy to avoid outages altogether; it describes resilience of service, not the safe state a single failed device should enter.

stem: An internal HR web application must become reachable to employees on the Internet without exposing the application server directly. The architect wants external connections terminated in a controlled zone, with inspection and authentication applied before requests reach the internal server. Which component fits this design?
options: A forward proxy configured in employees' browser settings
A NAT rule on the perimeter firewall publishing the server's internal address
A site-to-site VPN concentrator linking employees' home networks to the datacenter
A reverse proxy in a screened subnet that relays validated requests to the internal application
explanations: A forward proxy brokers outbound requests from internal clients to the Internet; the flow here is inbound users reaching an internal service, the reverse direction.
Static NAT merely forwards packets to the internal host, exposing the application directly with no session termination, inspection, or authentication in between.
Site-to-site VPNs join two fixed networks; employees on arbitrary Internet connections are not a fixed peer site, and a tunnel alone would neither proxy nor inspect application requests.
A reverse proxy terminates external sessions in a controlled zone, can enforce authentication and filtering, and originates a fresh connection inward, keeping the application server unexposed.

stem: Penetration testers stood up a rogue access point broadcasting the corporate SSID and harvested employees' 802.1X credentials when laptops attempted to authenticate through it. Which control BEST prevents corporate devices from disclosing credentials to such an evil twin?
options: Configure supplicants to validate the RADIUS server certificate against a pinned trusted CA and refuse authentication otherwise
Reduce access point transmit power so the corporate wireless signal does not extend beyond the building
Enforce a longer and more complex password policy for all wireless network users
Enable MAC address filtering so only corporate laptops can associate with the wireless network
explanations: The attack works because clients will authenticate to any infrastructure presenting the SSID; strict server-certificate validation (or moving to EAP-TLS) makes the supplicant reject the impostor's authentication server before any credential exchange occurs.
Transmit power shapes the legitimate network's footprint; the evil twin runs on the attacker's own radio, which corporate power settings cannot influence.
Longer passwords slow offline cracking, but the client still hands its authentication exchange to rogue infrastructure; the flaw is missing server authentication, not credential complexity.
MAC filtering governs which clients the corporate access points accept; it has no effect on which access points a client itself chooses to trust.

stem: Monitoring alerts that a switch's MAC address table filled with tens of thousands of entries learned from one access port, and the switch began flooding unicast frames out all ports, letting a connected host capture other users' traffic. Which control directly counters this attack?
options: Storm control thresholds for broadcast and multicast traffic volumes
Port security limiting the number of source MAC addresses learned per port
BPDU guard to shut down ports that receive spanning tree protocol messages
Dynamic ARP inspection validating address resolution messages on untrusted ports
explanations: Storm control rate-limits broadcast, multicast, or unknown-unicast volume; it does not prevent the table exhaustion that converts the switch into a hub in the first place.

The scenario is a CAM table overflow attack; capping learned source addresses per port, with a shutdown or restrict violation action, stops one station from exhausting the table and forcing flood behavior.
BPDU guard defends the spanning tree topology against rogue switches; this attacker sends forged data frames with random source addresses, not STP messages.
Dynamic ARP inspection blocks ARP cache poisoning, a different layer 2 attack; it does not limit how many MAC addresses a port may present.

stem: A network engineer proposes that switch, router, and firewall administration interfaces be reachable only from a physically separate management network rather than from the production LAN. What is the PRIMARY security benefit of this design?
options: It increases throughput by removing management traffic from busy production links
It lets administrators manage devices conveniently from any workstation in the enterprise
A compromised production host cannot reach device management planes, and administration remains possible during production network incidents
It eliminates the need for authentication on device interfaces since the management network is isolated
explanations: Freeing production bandwidth is a trivial side effect; management traffic volume is negligible, and performance is not a security rationale.
The design does the opposite: only stations on the management network can administer devices, because broad workstation reachability is exactly the exposure being removed.

Separating the management plane means malware on user or server segments has no path to infrastructure logins, and engineers keep out-of-band control of devices even when the production network is degraded or under attack.
Isolation is one defensive layer, not a substitute for authentication; defense in depth still requires strong credentials and logging on every management interface.

stem: Two internal microservices exchange sensitive account data across the datacenter network. Policy requires that each service verify the identity of the other before any data flows, in addition to encrypting the session. Which mechanism satisfies both requirements?
options: TLS with server certificates issued by the internal certificate authority
Mutual TLS in which each service presents and validates a certificate during the handshake
IP allowlists restricting which datacenter hosts may open connections to each service
Hashing each payload with SHA-256 before it is transmitted between the services
explanations: Standard TLS authenticates only the server side of the connection; the calling service's identity is never verified, leaving half of the requirement unmet.
mTLS performs certificate-based authentication in both directions during the handshake and then encrypts the channel, providing verified peer identity plus confidentiality in a single mechanism.
Address-based trust identifies a network location rather than a workload; addresses can be spoofed or shared by co-resident services, and an allowlist provides no encryption at all.
A digest provides integrity checking only; it authenticates neither party and leaves the account data itself unencrypted in transit.

stem: A company carries iSCSI storage traffic across the same converged datacenter network as ordinary server VLANs to reduce cabling costs. An auditor flags the design as exposing block storage to any compromised server. Which combination of measures BEST addresses the risk?
options: Enable jumbo frames and QoS tagging so storage traffic receives priority over user traffic
Isolate storage traffic on dedicated non-routed VLANs or a separate fabric, and require mutual CHAP authentication between initiators and targets
Replace iSCSI with Fibre Channel, since a dedicated FC fabric is immune to network-based attacks
Encrypt data at rest on the storage arrays so intercepted LUN traffic is unreadable to attackers
explanations: Jumbo frames and QoS improve storage performance on a converged fabric; they provide no confidentiality, authentication, or isolation whatsoever.

Because iSCSI carries raw block data with weak defaults, segregating it from general-purpose segments and mutually authenticating initiators and targets prevents unauthorized hosts from reaching or mounting LUNs.

Fibre Channel is not inherently immune; zoning misconfigurations and fabric attacks exist, and a rip-and-replace answers a design flaw with cost rather than the isolation and authentication actually required.
At-rest encryption protects the physical disks, but the array decrypts blocks before transmission, so iSCSI traffic on the shared network remains exposed in transit.

stem: An IPv4-only enterprise discovers workstations exfiltrating data through tunnels established after receiving rogue IPv6 router advertisements on the LAN, bypassing egress controls that inspect only IPv4. Which action BEST remediates this exposure?
options: Block protocol 41 encapsulation at the Internet perimeter so IPv6 packets cannot leave inside IPv4
Rely on the existing NAT boundary, since private internal addressing prevents hosts from reaching external tunnel endpoints
Enable RA Guard on access ports and bring IPv6 within egress policy and monitoring, disabling it where it is not needed
Deploy intrusion detection signatures that alert on traffic patterns of known IPv6 tunneling utilities
explanations: Filtering protocol 41 stops only one encapsulation method (6in4); tunnels over UDP such as Teredo, tunnels inside HTTPS, and rogue-RA traffic on the LAN itself are all unaffected.
Private IPv4 addressing is no barrier here: hosts obtained routable IPv6 configuration directly from the rogue advertisements, and address translation applies only to the IPv4 path.

The root cause is a protocol that is active by default on endpoints but absent from security policy; RA Guard blocks rogue advertisements at the switch port, and managing IPv6 under the same egress and monitoring controls as IPv4 closes the blind spot.
Signatures detect known tools after the fact; the underlying design gap, an unmanaged protocol outside all security controls, remains open for the next technique.

stem: A SOC relies on internal DNS resolver logs to detect malware command-and-control domains. Detections are dropping because many endpoints and browsers now resolve names via encrypted DNS over HTTPS directly to public providers. What should the security team do FIRST?
options: Decrypt all outbound HTTPS at the forward proxy so encrypted DNS queries become visible again
Accept encrypted DNS as a privacy improvement and retire the DNS-based detection content
Migrate detection to flow-record analysis, which does not depend on observing name resolution
Use endpoint and browser policy to direct managed devices to the enterprise resolver and block known external DoH services at egress
explanations: Universal TLS interception is a disproportionate first step: it is costly and privacy-sensitive, and pinned or unproxied DoH connections would still escape it; policy control of managed endpoints is simpler and targeted.

External encrypted resolution benefits personal privacy, but on corporate assets it removes a primary detection and control point; conceding the telemetry abandons the capability rather than restoring it.

Flow records show connections but not the queried names, discarding the domain intelligence that drives command-and-control detection; this substitutes weaker telemetry instead of fixing resolution paths.

Managed endpoints can be steered through group policy, browser settings, and canary-domain behavior to the internal resolver, and egress blocking of known DoH endpoints funnels resolution back through the monitored path with minimal disruption.

stem: A board meeting held on the company's video conferencing platform was joined by an uninvited participant who obtained the reusable meeting link from a forwarded email. Which combination of platform controls BEST prevents a recurrence for sensitive meetings?
options: Unique per-meeting links with authenticated join, waiting-room admission, and locking the session once attendees arrive
End-to-end encryption so the meeting's audio and video streams cannot be read in transit
Recording every sensitive session so any intrusion can be identified and reviewed afterward
A published policy stating that links for sensitive meetings must never be forwarded
explanations: The failure was admission control, a static credential embedded in a link; per-meeting identifiers, authenticated participants, host-controlled admission, and session locking each close part of that gap.
Encryption protects the media from network eavesdroppers; the intruder joined as a participant, so end-to-end encrypted streams would have been delivered to them like any attendee.
Recording is a detective control operating after the fact; the sensitive discussion is already exposed by the time any recording is reviewed.
Policy guides behavior, but the leak was an ordinary email forward; without technical admission controls a single human mistake still exposes the meeting.

stem: Two campus buildings are connected by a provider-delivered metro Ethernet circuit operating at layer 2. Security requires line-rate encryption of all traffic between the buildings, including non-IP protocols, with minimal added latency. Which technology BEST fits?
options: Site-to-site IPsec tunnels between routers placed at each building
MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) enabled on the switch interfaces facing the metro Ethernet link
TLS enforced for every application communicating across the inter-building link
PPTP tunnels established between the campus core switches at each site
explanations: IPsec encrypts IP packets only, so non-IP layer 2 traffic crossing the metro circuit would pass unprotected or require extra encapsulation, and per-packet router crypto adds latency compared with line-rate hardware.
802.1AE encrypts every Ethernet frame in hardware across the link, covering all protocols at wire speed with negligible latency, matching the layer at which the provider circuit actually operates.
Relying on each application's TLS leaves non-TLS protocols, management traffic, and legacy systems exposed; coverage would be partial and effectively unmanageable.
PPTP is an obsolete tunneling protocol with broken MS-CHAPv2 authentication and weak RC4-based encryption; it is unsuitable for any modern confidentiality requirement.

stem: During an architecture review, a network engineer argues that a branch office does not need a firewall because all hosts use RFC 1918 private addresses behind NAT, so outsiders cannot reach them anyway. What is the BEST response from the security architect?
options: Agree, because NAT hides internal addresses and drops unsolicited inbound packets by design
Require proxy ARP on the edge router to conceal internal MAC addresses from the Internet
Explain that NAT is an address translation mechanism, not a security control, and require a firewall enforcing explicit policy
Replace NAT with IPv6 global addressing so IPsec can be used end to end without translation
explanations: This treats a side effect of address translation as a designed security control. NAT's inbound behavior is incidental and is undermined by port forwarding, protocol helpers, or misconfiguration; it enforces no security policy.
This confuses layer 2 concealment with perimeter security. MAC addresses never traverse the Internet in the first place, and proxy ARP does nothing to control which traffic reaches internal hosts.
NAT exists to conserve and translate addresses; any filtering effect is incidental. Sound design requires an explicit policy-enforcement point, a firewall, regardless of the addressing scheme in use.

This confuses an addressing modernization project with a security fix. Moving to IPv6 with end-to-end IPsec is a long-term effort and still requires boundary policy enforcement; it does not close the immediate gap.

stem: An audit finds that administrators manage core switches over Telnet from their desktops, so device credentials cross the network in cleartext. Which remediation should the security team recommend FIRST?
options: Replace Telnet with SSH for all device management sessions
Enable SNMPv3 on the switches for configuration changes
Require administrators to change device passwords after every session
Move the switches to a separate VLAN so users cannot reach them
explanations: SSH provides encrypted, authenticated management sessions and is the direct replacement for Telnet, eliminating cleartext credential exposure with minimal operational change.
This confuses monitoring and polling with interactive management. SNMPv3 secures a different management channel and would not remove the cleartext Telnet sessions administrators still use.
This confuses credential rotation with transport protection. Passwords are still captured in cleartext during each session and can be used immediately by an eavesdropper.
This confuses segmentation with encryption. A management VLAN reduces who can sniff the traffic, but the credentials still cross the network unencrypted wherever the session travels.

stem: A legal team must email highly sensitive case files to outside counsel. The email gateway already negotiates opportunistic TLS with most partner domains. Why might the security officer still require S/MIME encryption for these messages?
options: TLS cannot encrypt attachments larger than the negotiated record size
TLS protects mail only between servers, while S/MIME keeps content encrypted end to end, including on relays and in mailboxes
S/MIME provides faster delivery because encrypted messages bypass content inspection at every relaying gateway
Opportunistic TLS always downgrades to cleartext when either mail server also supports S/MIME
explanations: This invents a TLS limitation. TLS fragments data across records transparently and imposes no attachment size constraint, so message size is not the reason to add S/MIME.

SMTP TLS is hop-by-hop: each mail server decrypts the message, so content sits in plaintext on every relay and in stored mailboxes. S/MIME encrypts the message object itself, protecting it from sender to recipient.
This confuses end-to-end encryption with a delivery optimization. S/MIME does not speed delivery, and bypassing gateway inspection is a side effect that must be managed, not a benefit.
This misstates TLS negotiation. Opportunistic TLS falls back to cleartext only when a peer lacks TLS support, which is unrelated to whether either party uses S/MIME.

stem: Penetration testers repeatedly exploit SQL injection in a public web application over HTTPS. Code fixes will take months to ship. Which network control BEST reduces this exposure in the meantime?
options: A stateful packet-filtering firewall restricting inbound traffic to TCP port 443
A network intrusion prevention system watching the encrypted sessions inline
A screened subnet separating the web tier from the database tier
A web application firewall terminating TLS and filtering application-layer requests
explanations: This confuses network-layer filtering with application-layer defense. The attack already arrives over the permitted port 443, so a layer 3/4 stateful firewall cannot tell malicious requests from legitimate ones.
This overlooks that a network IPS without TLS termination sees only ciphertext, so it cannot match injection patterns inside the encrypted sessions.
This confuses architectural containment with attack prevention. Tier separation limits blast radius, but injected queries still reach and execute against the database through the web tier.
A WAF decrypts and inspects HTTP requests, blocking injection patterns and virtually patching the flaw until code fixes ship, which is the appropriate compensating control at the application layer.

stem: Your company acquires a smaller firm, and executives want the two office networks fully joined within a week to speed integration. The acquired network's security posture is unknown. What should the security architect recommend FIRST?
options: Connect the networks only through a restrictive, monitored interconnect while the acquired environment is assessed
Merge the networks immediately and schedule a vulnerability scan of the acquired hosts for the following quarter
Extend the corporate zero trust policy engine across the acquired firm before allowing any connectivity
Require the acquired firm to re-address its network into the corporate IP plan before any traffic is exchanged
explanations: A limited, monitored interconnect delivers the connectivity the business needs while containing an environment of unknown posture, letting assessment and remediation proceed before broader trust is extended.
This inverts risk management by accepting full exposure first and assessing later. Any existing compromise in the acquired network could spread unchecked for months before the scan runs.

This confuses the desirable end state with a feasible first step. Deploying a zero trust policy engine across an unassessed, unmanaged estate takes far longer than the business will wait and still needs interim connectivity.
This confuses IP address planning with security due diligence. Re-addressing is integration hygiene; it neither evaluates nor contains the risk the unknown network presents.

stem: A security team notices its IDS misses sessions during peak hours. The sensor receives traffic from a switch SPAN port that is frequently oversubscribed. What is the BEST way to give the sensor complete visibility?
options: Configure an additional SPAN session on the same switch to share the mirroring load
Deploy a dedicated network TAP on the monitored link and feed the sensor from it
Move the sensor inline so the switch must forward every packet through it
Enable NetFlow export so the sensor can reconstruct the missing sessions
explanations: This misunderstands SPAN limits. Mirror sessions share the same switch fabric and egress capacity, so adding sessions compounds oversubscription rather than relieving it.
A passive TAP copies every frame on the link at line rate, independent of switch load, giving the sensor complete and unaltered visibility without affecting production traffic.
This confuses detection architecture with prevention. Moving inline converts the sensor into a potential bottleneck and failure point, changing the risk profile instead of simply fixing visibility.
This confuses flow telemetry with packet capture. NetFlow summarizes conversations as metadata and cannot reconstruct payloads the detection engine needs to inspect.

stem: A hotel wants guests to join Wi-Fi without accounts or passwords, but a review found the current open SSID lets anyone eavesdrop on guest traffic. Which option BEST addresses the eavesdropping while preserving the frictionless join experience?
options: Publish a shared WPA2-Personal passphrase on lobby signage so every guest device can encrypt its traffic
Add a captive portal so guests must accept terms before their traffic is allowed to flow
Enable Wi-Fi Enhanced Open (OWE) so each guest session is individually encrypted without authentication
Hide the SSID so only guests who are told the network name can associate
explanations: A publicly posted passphrase gives little protection: with WPA2-Personal, anyone holding the passphrase can derive another client's keys after observing its association, so eavesdropping remains practical.
This confuses acceptable-use gating with confidentiality. A captive portal controls access to the Internet but adds no encryption to the over-the-air traffic.

Opportunistic Wireless Encryption gives each client an individually encrypted session without requiring any credential, directly addressing eavesdropping while keeping the open-join experience guests expect.
This confuses obscurity with protection. A hidden SSID is trivially discovered from probe and association frames and does nothing to encrypt guest traffic.

stem: A configuration review shows routers and switches answer SNMP read and write requests using the community string 'private' from any source address. Which remediation BEST addresses the risk?
options: Change the community string to a long random value stored in the password vault
Disable SNMP entirely and rely on syslog for all device monitoring needs
Restrict SNMP to the management VLAN while keeping version 2c for tool compatibility
Migrate to SNMPv3 with authentication and privacy, and restrict sources to management hosts
explanations: This misses that SNMPv2c transmits the community string in cleartext. However random it is, anyone sniffing the path captures it and can immediately reuse it, including for write operations.
This overcorrects by removing a needed capability. Syslog is push-only event logging and cannot replace polling and managed configuration; secure SNMP exists precisely for this purpose.
This confuses reachability control with protocol security. Restricting sources helps, but v2c still sends credentials and data unencrypted, so anyone on the management path can read or replay them.

SNMPv3 with authentication and privacy adds per-user credentials and encryption, and source restriction adds defense in depth, addressing both the cleartext community string and the unrestricted write access.

stem: An external assessment reveals that the company's Internet-facing DNS server answers queries for internal hostnames, exposing the names and addresses of domain controllers and file servers. Which design change BEST corrects this?
options: Implement split DNS so external servers host only public records and internal zones stay on internal resolvers
Sign all zones with DNSSEC so external parties cannot read the internal records
Block TCP port 53 at the firewall so only small UDP queries reach the server
Rename internal hosts with unpredictable labels so leaked records reveal nothing useful
explanations: Split DNS separates the namespace: Internet-facing servers publish only records that must be public, while internal zones resolve only on internal resolvers, removing the reconnaissance exposure by design.
This confuses integrity with confidentiality. DNSSEC signs records so responses can be validated; it does not hide them, and signed zones can be even easier to enumerate.
This confuses transport blocking with data separation. TCP port 53 relates to zone transfers and large responses; the internal records would still be answered over ordinary UDP queries.
This relies on obscurity. Unpredictable names complicate administration, yet the records remain publicly resolvable and still leak live internal addresses once observed.

stem: Threat intelligence indicates an adversary is recording the company's encrypted VPN traffic for later analysis, and the concentrator's private key could plausibly be stolen in the future. Which property MOST directly limits the damage from that scenario?
options: Longer RSA keys on the concentrator certificate to make factoring computationally infeasible
Forward secrecy from ephemeral key agreement, so past sessions cannot be decrypted with the stolen key
Certificate pinning on clients so a stolen key cannot be used to impersonate the gateway
Rotating the concentrator certificate quarterly so any stolen key ages out quickly
explanations: This addresses the wrong threat. Key length defends against cryptanalysis of the key; it is irrelevant when the private key itself is exfiltrated intact.
With ephemeral Diffie-Hellman agreement, each session's keys are independent of the server's long-term key, so recorded ciphertext remains undecryptable even after the private key is later stolen.
This confuses authentication with confidentiality of recorded traffic. Pinning constrains which certificates clients accept on future connections; it does nothing for ciphertext already captured.
This confuses shrinking the exposure window with eliminating it. Every session recorded before a rotation would still be decryptable if those key exchanges depended on the compromised key.

stem: A manufacturer is cabling a new production floor filled with large motors and welding equipment. Data errors from electrical interference are a major concern, and cable runs pass through areas open to visiting contractors. Which transmission medium BEST fits these conditions?
options: Shielded twisted pair, because grounding the shield eliminates all induced noise
Coaxial cable, because its solid core resists vibration from heavy machinery
Fiber optic cable, because it is immune to electromagnetic interference and difficult to tap unnoticed
Unshielded twisted pair at a higher category rating, because faster cable rejects interference
explanations: This overstates what shielding does. STP attenuates induced noise but cannot eliminate it in a high-EMI environment, and copper remains susceptible to inductive tapping.
This confuses mechanical robustness with electrical immunity. Coax still carries electrical signals subject to EMI and can be tapped with simple hardware.
Light-based transmission is unaffected by electromagnetic fields from motors and welders, and tapping fiber generally requires physically disturbing the cable in ways that are detectable.
This confuses bandwidth category with interference immunity. Higher-category UTP improves signal characteristics but remains an unshielded electrical medium vulnerable to EMI.

stem: A hospital's 802.1X deployment cannot cover infusion pumps and badge printers that lack supplicant support, so those switch ports use MAC Authentication Bypass. The CISO asks how the risk MAB introduces should be handled. What is the BEST response?
options: MAB is equivalent to certificate authentication because the RADIUS server validates each MAC address
Disable MAB and leave those ports unauthenticated since the devices are trusted medical equipment
Replace every non-supplicant device immediately regardless of clinical replacement cycles
Keep MAB but place those devices in tightly restricted VLANs with ACLs and monitor for MAC spoofing
explanations: This overstates MAB's assurance. A MAC address is an identifier, not a secret; it is visible on the wire and trivially spoofed, so checking it against a list is weak authentication at best.
This abandons a control instead of managing its weakness, leaving the ports open to any device that plugs in, which is a worse position than compensated MAB.
This ignores operational and clinical reality. Medical devices follow long replacement cycles and budgets; risk management calls for compensating controls in the interim, not an impractical mandate.
This is sound risk treatment: retain the necessary but weaker control, constrain what those segments can reach with restricted VLANs and ACLs, and add detection for the residual spoofing risk.

stem: A company plans to deploy TLS interception on its web proxy to inspect outbound traffic for data loss and malware. The privacy officer raises concerns about employees' personal banking and health sites. What is the BEST way to proceed?
options: Inspect by default but bypass decryption for defined categories such as financial and health sites, and disclose the practice to employees
Inspect all traffic uniformly because selective bypass would create blind spots attackers could exploit
Abandon interception and rely on DNS-based filtering so employee content is never decrypted
Inspect all traffic but retain decrypted content for only thirty days to limit privacy exposure
explanations: Category-based bypass balances the inspection objective against legal and privacy obligations for sensitive personal traffic, and disclosure to employees addresses consent and policy transparency requirements.

This treats inspection coverage as an absolute and ignores privacy and legal constraints. Many jurisdictions and policies expect sensitive personal categories such as banking and health to be excluded from decryption.
This overcorrects. DNS filtering blocks known-bad domains but cannot inspect content for data loss or embedded malware, abandoning the control's core objectives entirely.
This confuses retention minimization with collection minimization. The privacy concern is decrypting the sensitive sessions at all, not how long the decrypted results are stored.

stem: Twice this month the network went down after employees plugged unmanaged desktop switches into wall jacks, triggering spanning tree recalculations and a bridging loop. Which control BEST prevents a recurrence at the access layer?
options: Increase the core switches' spanning tree priority so they always remain the root bridge
Enable BPDU Guard on access ports so any port receiving bridge protocol messages is shut down
Enable port security so ports that learn more than one MAC address are disabled
Deploy DHCP snooping so devices behind rogue switches cannot obtain addresses
explanations: This confuses root placement with edge protection. A stable root bridge does not stop unauthorized switches from injecting BPDUs, forcing topology changes, or creating loops at the edge.

BPDU Guard error-disables any access port that receives a bridge protocol data unit, the signature of a connected switch, stopping both topology manipulation and user-created loops at the point of entry.

This confuses MAC-count enforcement with loop prevention. Port security targets address-table abuse; a rogue switch with a single active device behind it may never violate the MAC limit yet still cause a loop.
This confuses address-assignment protection with layer 2 loop control. DHCP snooping polices DHCP messages and has no effect on spanning tree behavior or bridging loops.

stem: An enterprise is moving its data center to a software-defined network in which a central controller programs all switching behavior through southbound APIs. During threat modeling, which risk should receive the HIGHEST priority?
options: Loss of a single leaf switch, because SDN cannot reroute around failed hardware
Encrypted east-west traffic, because inspection tools cannot read flows between virtual machines
Compromise of the controller or its APIs, because it would grant an attacker authority over the entire network's forwarding behavior
Vendor lock-in from proprietary northbound applications, because migration costs would rise
explanations: This misunderstands SDN, which typically improves failure response: the controller reprograms paths around failed hardware, so a single leaf loss is an availability event of limited scope.
This is a genuine monitoring challenge but a second-order one. Reduced inspection visibility does not compare with an adversary gaining programmatic control of forwarding itself.

The controller concentrates the network's entire control plane. Compromising it or its APIs lets an attacker reroute, mirror, or black-hole any traffic, a single point whose failure mode is total, so it warrants top priority.
This confuses a procurement concern with a security threat. Vendor lock-in affects cost and flexibility, not the confidentiality or integrity of traffic under threat modeling.

stem: An office of 300 staff uses one WPA2-Personal passphrase for the corporate SSID. After several departures the passphrase has never changed, because updating every device is disruptive. Which change BEST resolves the underlying problem?
options: Adopt a longer passphrase and rotate it every ninety days through the MDM platform
Move the corporate network to a hidden SSID so former employees cannot find it
Enable MAC address filtering so only inventoried corporate devices can associate
Migrate to WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise so each user authenticates individually and access ends when accounts are disabled
explanations: This treats the symptom. Rotation still leaves one shared secret for every user, each rotation remains disruptive, and between rotations departed staff retain working access.
This confuses hiding the network with revoking access. Former employees already know the SSID, and hidden networks are trivially rediscovered from client probe traffic.
This confuses device identification with authentication. MAC addresses are easily observed over the air and spoofed, and maintaining the list for hundreds of devices is unmanageable.
Enterprise mode uses 802.1X to authenticate each user or device with individual directory credentials, so offboarding automatically ends wireless access without reconfiguring anyone else's device.

stem: During an external scan, testers download the company's entire DNS zone using an AXFR request against the authoritative name server, revealing every registered host. What is the BEST corrective action?
options: Restrict zone transfers to the specific addresses of authorized secondary name servers
Disable recursion on the authoritative server so it answers only for its own zones
Shorten the zone's TTL values so any leaked records expire quickly
Place the name server behind a load balancer so AXFR sessions cannot complete
explanations: Zone transfers exist to replicate data to secondary servers; limiting AXFR to their specific addresses, ideally with transaction signatures, preserves that function while denying bulk reconnaissance to everyone else.
This confuses recursive resolution with zone replication. Recursion settings govern lookups performed on behalf of clients; AXFR requests are answered from authoritative data regardless.
This confuses cache lifetime with disclosure. TTL controls how long resolvers cache answers; it neither prevents the transfer nor makes the enumerated hosts any less exposed.
This misapplies load balancing. A load balancer distributes sessions; it does not evaluate DNS operation types, and a transfer would simply complete against whichever backend receives it.

stem: A defense contractor sends sensitive traffic between two sites over a carrier service advertised as fully encrypted. The security architect learns each carrier node decrypts and re-encrypts traffic as it forwards it. What is the MOST appropriate conclusion?
options: The design is acceptable because traffic is never exposed on any physical wire between nodes
Link encryption leaves plaintext exposed inside intermediate nodes, so the contractor should add end-to-end encryption it controls
The carrier should be asked to add a second layer of link encryption at each hop for defense in depth
The design fails only if the carrier's nodes are located outside the contractor's home country
explanations: This overlooks node exposure. Link encryption protects only the spans between devices; at every intermediate node the traffic exists in plaintext, accessible to carrier staff or through a node compromise.

This is the classic link versus end-to-end distinction: hop-by-hop encryption decrypts at each node, so data the contractor cannot afford to expose needs encryption applied at endpoints under its own control.
This misapplies defense in depth. Stacking additional link-layer encryption changes nothing at the decryption points inside each node, which is where the exposure actually occurs.
This confuses jurisdictional risk with architectural exposure. Plaintext inside intermediate nodes is a design weakness wherever the nodes sit; location only changes who might exploit it.

stem: A hospital plans to deploy an inline IPS on the network segment carrying real-time patient telemetry. Engineers must choose the appliance's behavior if it loses power or crashes. Which configuration BEST reflects sound risk management?
options: Fail closed, because blocking all traffic during a failure prevents any attack from passing uninspected
Fail closed, but issue clinicians a procedure to physically re-cable around the appliance during outages
Fail open with a hardware bypass, because interrupting patient telemetry poses a greater risk than briefly uninspected traffic
Fail open permanently by running the sensor in passive SPAN mode so it can never affect traffic
explanations: This applies fail-secure reasoning without weighing consequence. On a life-safety segment, total loss of telemetry during a failure creates direct patient risk that outweighs a short period of uninspected traffic.
This underestimates the outage impact. Manual re-cabling takes minutes at best, real-time telemetry cannot tolerate that gap, and improvised procedures performed under pressure invite further error.

Risk management weighs the consequence of each failure mode: for real-time patient telemetry, availability is safety-critical, so a hardware bypass that preserves flow during sensor failure is the defensible choice, paired with alerting.
This overcorrects by abandoning prevention entirely. Passive mode turns the device into an IDS that can never block; the goal is to keep inline prevention while engineering a safe failure mode.

stem: An ISP notifies a company that packets bearing other organizations' source addresses are leaving its network as part of a reflection DDoS campaign. Which control at the Internet edge BEST prevents the company's network from being misused this way?
options: Inbound rate limiting on the border router to blunt reflected replies arriving from the campaign
Blackhole routing that discards all traffic destined for the DDoS victims' address ranges
RPKI route origin validation so forged BGP announcements are rejected at the border
Egress filtering that drops outbound packets whose source addresses are not from the company's assigned ranges
explanations: This addresses the wrong direction. The abuse is spoofed traffic leaving the network; inbound rate limiting shapes what arrives and does nothing about forged outbound source addresses.
This confuses victim-side response with source hygiene. Blackholing discards traffic toward the victims; it does not stop the company's hosts from originating spoofed packets in the first place.
This confuses routing integrity with packet-source validation. RPKI verifies BGP route origins; it cannot detect or drop individual data packets carrying forged source addresses.

Egress source-address filtering ensures only packets from the organization's legitimate ranges leave the network, the anti-spoofing hygiene long recommended as BCP 38, which removes its role in reflection attacks.

stem: A quarterly review finds a firewall rule permitting any source to any destination on all ports, added during a troubleshooting session eight months earlier and forgotten. What does this finding MOST clearly indicate is missing?
options: A change management process with expiration and periodic recertification of firewall rules
A next-generation firewall, since legacy platforms cannot express granular policies
An intrusion prevention system to compensate for the overly permissive rule
Separation of duties so firewall administrators cannot approve their own emergency changes
explanations: A troubleshooting rule that survives eight months reveals absent lifecycle governance: emergency changes should carry expirations, and periodic rule recertification should catch anything that slips through.
This confuses product capability with process failure. Any firewall can express granular rules; the problem is that an overly broad rule was created and never reviewed or removed.
This proposes a compensating control instead of fixing the root cause. An IPS might reduce exploitation, but the finding demonstrates a governance gap, not a missing detection layer.
This overreaches from the evidence. Separation of duties concerns who approves changes; the demonstrated failure is that no process expired or recertified the rule after the emergency passed.

stem: Facilities installs a point-to-point wireless bridge to link two office buildings across a public street, replacing a leased line. What additional safeguard is MOST important before carrying corporate traffic over the bridge?
options: Narrow-beam directional antennas so the signal cannot be received away from the path
Strong encryption of all traffic crossing the bridge, since the radio signal extends beyond company control
MAC address filtering so only the two bridge radios can associate with each other
Reduced transmit power so the link cannot be detected from street level
explanations: This mistakes propagation control for protection. Directional antennas reduce stray signal, but sidelobes and sensitive receivers can still intercept it, and interception attempts are undetectable.
The medium is broadcast into space the company does not control, so confidentiality must come from strong modern encryption of the link rather than assumptions about who can receive the signal.
This confuses device identification with confidentiality. MAC filtering encrypts nothing, and the bridge radios' addresses are visible over the air and easily spoofed.
This confuses lowering detectability with securing content. Reduced power mainly degrades the link's reliability, and a properly positioned receiver can still capture and record the signal.

stem: Security policy forbids unauthorized wireless access points, but a walkthrough discovered an employee-installed AP wired into a conference room jack. Management wants continuous detection rather than periodic walkthroughs. Which control BEST meets that goal?
options: Quarterly wireless penetration tests covering every office location
A NAC agent on corporate laptops that reports nearby SSIDs to a central console
A wireless intrusion prevention system with sensors that continuously scan for rogue devices
An annual review of switch CAM tables for unrecognized MAC addresses
explanations: This confuses periodic assurance with continuous detection. Quarterly tests leave months during which a rogue access point can operate unnoticed.
This yields incidental, incomplete coverage. Laptop-based scanning observes only where laptops happen to be powered on and misses areas and hours without them.
A WIPS uses dedicated sensors that continuously monitor the airspace, correlate observed access points against the authorized list, and can alert on or contain rogue devices in real time.
This confuses a point-in-time wired audit with wireless monitoring. An annual CAM review is far from continuous, and a rogue AP's wired MAC address rarely identifies it as an access point.

stem: Weeks after moving to SIP trunking, a company receives a massive bill for international calls placed overnight through its IP-PBX. Investigation finds Internet-exposed SIP registration protected only by weak extension passwords. Which combination MOST effectively prevents recurrence?
options: Enable SRTP on all calls so attackers cannot listen to the fraudulent conversations
Move the PBX behind NAT so external endpoints can no longer send packets to it
Publish the trunk on a nonstandard port so scanners stop finding the registration service
Restrict signaling to the provider's addresses, enforce strong authentication over TLS, and set toll restrictions with alerts
explanations: This confuses media confidentiality with access control. SRTP encrypts call audio; it does nothing to stop unauthorized parties from registering extensions and placing calls.
This treats NAT as a security control. Translation authenticates no one, and SIP deployments typically require traversal mechanisms that keep the service reachable anyway.
This is security through obscurity. Internet-wide scanners sweep all ports quickly, and the weak authentication remains fully exploitable the moment the service is found.

Layered controls address the actual failure chain: source restriction removes Internet-wide exposure, strong authentication over TLS protects credentials, and toll restrictions with alerting cap the financial damage of any future compromise.

stem: A retailer offloads its storefront to a CDN that terminates TLS at global edge nodes. An architect discovers the CDN fetches content from the origin data center over plain HTTP because that connection is considered trusted. What is the MOST significant issue?
options: Customers' browsers will display certificate warnings because the edge certificate does not match the origin
CDN caching will serve stale pages because HTTP responses cannot carry cache-control headers
Traffic between the CDN edge and the origin crosses the Internet unencrypted, exposing sessions and data despite the padlock users see
TLS termination at the edge violates PCI DSS, which requires encryption to terminate only inside the cardholder environment
explanations: This misunderstands the TLS topology. Browsers negotiate with the edge and see a valid edge certificate; the insecure back-end leg is invisible to them, which is precisely what makes it dangerous.
This invents an HTTP limitation. Cache-control headers function over plain HTTP, so caching behavior is unrelated to the transport-security gap.

The padlock attests only to the browser-to-edge segment. The edge-to-origin fetch crosses untrusted networks in cleartext, exposing session data and content, so that leg must be encrypted and the origin should authenticate the CDN.
This misreads PCI DSS, which requires strong cryptography over open public networks. Edge termination itself is acceptable; it is the unencrypted origin pull that would breach the requirement.
